questions.q: Describe the technique and achievements of Indian bronze sculpture, with special reference to the Chola Nataraja.

answer.text: Indian bronze images were cast by the lost-wax process, known as cire perdue. A model was first made in wax, coated with clay, and then heated so the wax flowed out, leaving a hollow mould into which molten metal was poured. This tradition began as early as the Dancing Girl of the Indus Valley and continued for thousands of years.
The finest Indian bronzes were made under the Cholas of Tamil Nadu. Their images are admired for grace, balance and lifelike modelling, and were carried in temple processions.

The most celebrated is the Nataraja, Shiva as the Lord of Dance, shown in the vigorous ananda tandava pose within a ring of flames, holding a drum and fire, and trampling the dwarf Apasmara, who stands for ignorance. It symbolises the cosmic rhythm of creation and destruction.

answer: Thus Chola bronzes represent the peak of this art.

questions.q: How does the Chola Nataraja bronze express religious ideas through art?

answer.text: shows Shiva as the Lord of Dance, and it is a masterpiece in which every element carries meaning.

list: The dance within a ring of flames represents the cosmos and the endless cycle of creation and destruction
The drum in one hand stands for the sound of creation; the fire in another for destruction
One hand is raised in protection, and a foot is lifted to promise release to the devotee

answer.text: The graceful, balanced figure embodies deep ideas.

list: The dwarf under Shiva's foot is ignorance being crushed
The whole image turns a religious idea into perfect, moving sculpture

questions.q: How was the lost-wax technique used to cast bronze images in South India?

answer.text: especially under the Cholas, were made by the difficult and skilful lost-wax (cire perdue) method.

list: The artist first made a detailed model of the image in wax
This was covered with clay and left to dry, with small openings left in the mould

answer.lead: Then the metal replaced the wax.

list: The mould was heated so the wax melted and flowed out, leaving a hollow
Molten bronze was poured in to fill the space; when cool, the clay was broken to reveal the image, which was then finished and polished
